An Instagram video shows her bewildering encounter with far more flatulence than anybody could’ve bargained for. When Stone asked the human safety driver — who Tesla is required to have behind the wheel as the company’s robotaxis are not licensed in California yet — why the car kept farting, he shrugged and replied “no idea.” “That’s crazy!” a baffled Stone can be heard saying, while stifling laughter. The driver said he was playing with the settings, only to lose control of the feature. “It’s the first time I’m experiencing this,” he said. “Sorry.” “Even the volume doesn’t control it,” the driver added, laughing. The incident is particularly hilarious considering Tesla is trying to roll out a fully autonomous ride-hailing service in the country. Considering how controlling an eight-year-old prank feature is proving a little too challenging, it’s anybody’s guess what else could go wrong as the EV company lets software take the reins. We’ve already seen plenty of reports of terrifying close calls, crashes, and shoddy service . Most recently, Musk admitted that the company’s software — which relies entirely on cameras, and not LIDAR or radar sensors — struggled not to “run over pets” at night. And the changes go beyond NASA's public-facing communications, with at least one planned technical update described as "a breaking change" expected to disrupt existing software integrations. The terminology shift arrives as NASA continues expanding its use of AI across missions and research programs, from autonomous Mars rover navigation to models capable of analyzing enormous amounts of scientific data. The technologies themselves aren't changing, but NASA's effort to implement the nomenclature introduces new obstacles for scientific communication and the agency's digital infrastructure. candidates.title: Ancient warmth helped flowering plants dominate Earth, study finds
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Extreme global warmth drove both mass extinctions and explosions in plant diversity during two periods over the past 140 million years, offering new insights into how flowering plants became dominant on Earth, a new study has found.

The study examined fossilized pollen and spores to show that the mid-Cretaceous and early Cenozoic periods of extreme global warmth were central to plant evolution, both for flowering plants and the other main types on Earth, according to a statement released on Thursday by Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).

Researchers said that land plants sustain almost all terrestrial animals, fungi and bacteria, while flowering plants are the most productive and diverse group, with about 400,000 species worldwide.

The team examined more than 60,000 fossil occurrences and applied methods that overcome the major biases in the fossil record, generating revised estimates of fossil pollen and spore diversity over the past 130 million years, according to the study published in Nature Plants.

Both plant extinctions and the emergence of new but evolutionarily related plant groups occurred mostly during the two periods of extreme global warmth, said the study's co-author, UTAS Professor Greg Jordan.

Each interval lasted several million years, with warming simultaneously destroying and promoting plant diversity "over million-year timescales," Jordan said. In contrast, cooler periods were marked by little change in plant diversity.

However, the researchers warned that human-driven warming is likely to cause plant extinctions much faster than past extreme warming events.

candidates.title: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
candidates.raw_excerpt: On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn , with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017 . Running low on fuel, NASA chose to steer Cassini straight into Saturn's atmosphere, where the spacecraft was destroyed . NASA's Cassini spacecraft lifts off on Oct. 15, 1997, atop a Titan IVB rocket. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered NASA's Cassini mission to Saturn (which carried the European Space Agency's Huygens lander to Titan) was a flagship planetary mission like no other ever when it first launched toward the ringed planet. The $3.26 billion Cassini spacecraft became the first probe ever to orbit Saturn when it arrived in 2004. It revealed Saturn's rings as active and dynamic structures, as intricate and complex as they are beautiful to observe. And it delivered Huygens to Titan, then followed up with a series of Titan flybys that revealed the cloudy moon could have liquid hydrocarbon rain, rivers, lakes and seas. Perhaps the most exciting discoveries were the most surprising. Cassini discovered a strange hexagon-shaped jetstream encircling Saturn's north pole and revealed massive hurricane-like vortexes over both of the planet's poles. In 2010, Cassini watched as a giant storm formed in Saturn's northern hemisphere, then grew to encircle the entire planet through 2011. The spacecraft also discovered icy plumes of water erupting from Saturn's moon Enceladus , revealing new clues into that moon's subsurface ocean of liquid water, complete with hydrothermal events

The system swaps batteries in about 25 seconds, with DJI saying the Matrice 5TD aircraft can relaunch within 45 seconds. The drone flies for up to 59 minutes per sortie. The hardware bundle costs 167,999 yuan (about $25,000). Software subscriptions, site deployment and support services cost extra.

GizmoChina, a blog focused on Chinese and international tech, was less impressed, saying the system is "too expensive." The Gadgeteer warned that the 45-second turnaround was measured under controlled conditions and may vary with weather and installation.

The main overseas controversy is market access. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) added DJI to its Covered List in 2025 – a blacklist of communications equipment deemed a national security risk. Products on the list cannot receive FCC authorization.

(Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) A new image from the European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft reveals the powerful erosive forces that have shaped and re-shaped the surface of the Red Planet over long periods of geological time. What is it? This new Mars Express image captures Amazonis Mensa, a large, flat mountain on the Red Planet that offers planetary scientists a glimpse into the many factors that can sculpt a world's surface. In this photograph, several features stand out to help illustrate this. Easiest to make out are the large round craters created by ancient impacts on the surface of Mars . However, many of these craters have been at least partially filled by lava flowing across the surface of the Red Planet around three billion years ago, according a statement from the European Space Agency (ESA) accompanying the image. More interestingly, rippled structures known as yardangs can be seen to the left and right sides of the image. These ridges "form as loose sand particles are whipped up by wind and deployed a little like a cosmic sandblaster," according to ESA. In the image, the two groups of yardangs ripple across the Martian surface in two different directions. This is because Amazonis Mensa acts as a windbreak, pushing material blown by winds in separate orientations. Why is it incredible? For over 20 years, Mars Express has been providing scientists with an unparalleled look at the Martian surface, helping us better understand the forces that have shaped the Red Planet over eons.

Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML said on Wednesday that it is exploring ways to expand production capacity beyond the previously announced 30% increase planned for 2028, as growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI) drives stronger demand for its equipment.

"With such strong visibility and an order book momentum that continues to increase quarter on quarter this year, we now expect that our supply as currently planned for both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers," Fouquet said.

"So we have to do more, and we are looking basically at ways, especially in 2028 and beyond, to further extend our capacity," he added.

ASML reported total net sales of 11.7 billion euros (about $13.09 billion) in the third quarter of 2026, up 25% from the previous quarter. Net income reached nearly 5 billion euros in the third quarter.

The company expected full-year 2026 net sales of between 44 billion and 45 billion euros, with a gross margin of around 56%, Fouquet announced.

A newly discovered Jurassic bird from southeastern China is challenging the long-held view that early bird evolution was driven mainly by the need to fly.

Named Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, the species was identified by researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and the Fujian Institute of Geological Sciences. The findings were published in the journal Nature on October 14.

The fossil was discovered in August 2024 in Yangyuan Township, Zhenghe County, southeast China's Fujian Province. Weighing about 821 grams, the animal had a striking mix of bird-like and dinosaur-like features. Most notably, its forelimbs were unusually short, while its feet retained a specialized second toe characteristic of Deinonychosauria dinosaurs.

Comprehensive skeletal and phylogenetic analyses confirmed that the animal was a bird, not a non-avian dinosaur. Further analyses suggest it was a carnivore adapted to terrestrial life and incapable of flight.

For decades, scientists have regarded selection for flight as a major driver of early bird evolution. However, the scarcity of Jurassic bird fossils has left significant gaps in understanding how the characteristic bird body plan emerged.

candidates.title: China launches eight satellites for space-based computing
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China successfully launched eight satellites for a space-based computing project on Wednesday aboard the Zhuque-2E rocket, developed by the commercial space company LandSpace.

The mission carried 10 satellites in total and lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Test Zone in northwest China. The other two satellites were laser-communication test satellites developed by Lanta Intelligence. All 10 satellites entered their planned orbits.

The eight satellites make up the second batch of the space-based computing project dubbed “Xing Suan.” They carry high-performance computing payloads, high-speed laser communication systems linking satellites to one another and to the ground, and low-light cameras.

Developed by the Chinese commercial satellite company ADA Space, the new group will test several key technologies, including a liquid-cooling system at the 10-kilowatt scale, large deployable radiative-cooling wings, a laser communication network, and foundation-model training in orbit. 

These tests will help assess how data can be processed in orbit while maintaining reliable computing performance, managing heat, and transferring information efficiently.

Traditionally, large volumes of satellite data are transmitted back to Earth for processing. Onboard computing could enable more data to be analyzed in space before results are sent to the ground, potentially reducing transmission demands and delays while supporting applications in artificial intelligence and remote sensing.
